title: Self-representation: Fabricated authorities still attract accountability
desc: Separates citation misconduct from pleading failure and issue preservation, rejecting the idea that liberal treatment excuses fabricated AI authorities.

kps.k: Self-representation does not shield litigants from accountability for fabricated AI-generated authorities.
kps.d: In Al-Hamim v. Star Hearthstone, the court identifies fake cases in the tenant’s opening brief and warns that future filings containing nonexistent opinions, quotations and citations may attract sanctions. It invokes Mata v. Avianca’s account of attorneys abandoning their responsibilities when submitting ChatGPT-generated authorities. The practical implication is that self-represented litigants, as well as lawyers, must check authorities before filing. The supplied passages establish a prospective warning, not the sanctions disposition in Al-Hamim’s own case; they also provide no measure of model hallucination rates.

kps.k: The court separates citation misconduct from the substantive reasons for dismissing the tenant’s claims.
kps.d: The habitability ruling rests on missing allegations of material interference with life, health or safety under the statute applicable when the complaint was filed—not a categorical conclusion that animal contamination cannot breach habitability. The court distinguishes precedent involving pervasive urine odor, physical symptoms and other defects. For quiet enjoyment, it finds that inconvenience, delayed settling-in and strained cotenant relationships did not establish interference with possession: the complaint alleged neither inability to use the premises nor constructive eviction. These grounds should not be recast as dismissal because of AI hallucinations.

kps.k: Liberal interpretation of self-represented filings does not replace adequate pleading or preservation of issues.
kps.d: The court acknowledges its duty to interpret Al-Hamim’s filings liberally but excludes his later assertion that the carpet prevented bedroom use because he omitted it from the complaint. It also declines to consider new contract, fraud and negligence claims raised on appeal rather than deciding their merits. The central tension is between accommodating self-representation and maintaining procedural requirements, not a documented disagreement among sources. For AI-assisted legal self-help, the practical lesson extends beyond citation verification: litigants still need to plead legally material facts and raise claims at the proper stage.

vlens.an: The judicial source supports the proposition directly. It treats self-representation as no shield against accountability for fabricated authorities, while carefully limiting that conclusion to a prospective sanctions warning rather than claiming that sanctions were imposed in this case. It also distinguishes citation misconduct from the independent grounds for dismissal: deficient substantive allegations and ordinary pleading and issue-preservation rules. The material internal nuance is therefore about scope, not disagreement—the court interprets self-represented filings liberally, but does not allow that accommodation to cure omitted allegations or permit new claims on appeal. Because this is a curated source from one court, it establishes that court’s approach and should not be treated as evidence of prevalence across regulators, courts and professional bodies generally.

elens.an: The 2023–2024 source directly supports the proposition that self-representation does not excuse fabricated AI-generated authorities. The court identifies fake citations and gives prospective notice that similar future filings may attract sanctions, extending accountability beyond lawyers to self-represented litigants. It also keeps citation misconduct analytically separate from the merits: dismissal rested on deficient allegations concerning habitability and quiet enjoyment and on ordinary pleading and issue-preservation rules. Liberal interpretation accommodated the litigant’s status but did not allow omitted allegations or newly raised appellate claims to cure the complaint. The principal qualification is that the source documents a prospective sanctions warning, not the imposition of sanctions in Al-Hamim’s case. Because the evidence consists of one selected decision, it establishes that court’s approach rather than the prevalence of that approach across courts during the period.
